placeholders.name: COMPANY NAME
placeholders.what: Your business's actual name, exactly as you'd want it to appear in writing Claude produces. This anchors every draft in your real identity instead of a generic 'the company.'
examples: Rivera Consulting
Northwind Bakery
Alden & Cole Legal Services

placeholders.name: ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS
placeholders.what: A single sentence describing what your business does and for whom. Keep it factual and specific rather than a marketing tagline — Claude uses this to understand context, not to quote it back to customers.
examples: a boutique accounting firm serving small manufacturers
an online store selling handmade leather goods to individual customers
a 6-person marketing agency specializing in B2B software companies

placeholders.name: PRIMARY AUDIENCE, e.g. "mid-market CFOs evaluating software"
placeholders.what: The specific group of people who will read most of what this project produces. Precision matters — 'customers' is too broad to calibrate tone against, while 'busy restaurant owners deciding on a POS system' tells Claude exactly who it's writing for.
examples: small-business owners with no HR background, often first-time managers
existing clients renewing an annual service contract
prospective home buyers browsing listings for the first time

placeholders.name: e.g. "confident, plain-spoken, lightly warm — never salesy"
placeholders.what: Describe your brand's voice in 3-5 adjectives or a short phrase, paired with something it should NOT sound like. This appears next to the 'Tone:' label — the contrast between what it is and isn't pins down tone far more precisely than adjectives alone.
examples: calm and reassuring, never alarmist — we're the adults in the room
witty and a little irreverent, but never mean or sarcastic at a customer's expense
precise and technical but never condescending to non-experts

placeholders.name: PREFERRED TERM
placeholders.what: A specific word or phrase your brand always uses in place of a common alternative. This locks in consistent terminology across every chat in the project.
examples: clients
members
the platform

placeholders.name: BANNED TERM
placeholders.what: The word or phrase your preferred term replaces — something you never want to see in your brand's writing. Pair it directly with its preferred replacement so the rule is unambiguous.
examples: customers
users
the app

placeholders.name: REQUIRED ELEMENT, e.g. "a single clear call to action"
placeholders.what: Something that must appear in every piece of customer-facing copy this project produces, without exception. Naming it here means Claude never forgets it, even under a rushed one-line request.
examples: a single clear call to action at the end
our support email in case of questions
a one-line disclaimer that results vary

placeholders.name: LIST BANNED WORDS/PHRASES, e.g. "synergy, game-changing, unlock"
placeholders.what: The specific hype words or clichés you've decided your brand never uses. Most people can name three or four instantly — the words that make you cringe when a competitor uses them.
examples: revolutionary, disrupt, cutting-edge, best-in-class
seamless, world-class, take it to the next level
hustle, grind, crush it

variations.label: Minimal version for a solo freelancer
variations.whenToUse: Use this shorter instruction block when you're a one-person operation and don't need separate voice/audience/hard-rules sections spelled out in full detail.
variations.prompt: You're my writing assistant for [BUSINESS NAME], a [ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION]. I write mostly for [AUDIENCE]. My tone: [TONE, e.g. "direct, a little informal, no corporate speak"]. Never invent details about my services, prices, or past clients — if something isn't in the project knowledge or my message, ask me. Match the style of any sample documents I upload over these instructions.

variations.label: Multilingual / multi-market brand instructions
variations.whenToUse: Use when your project needs to produce content in more than one language or for more than one regional market, and tone or terms differ by market.
variations.prompt:
You are the writing assistant for [COMPANY NAME], a [ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS] operating in [MARKETS, e.g. "the UK and Germany"].

For each piece I ask for, first confirm which market and language it's for, since our voice differs slightly: [MARKET A] is [TONE A]; [MARKET B] is [TONE B].

Hard rules that apply everywhere: [UNIVERSAL RULES, e.g. "never state prices without currency; never use idioms that don't translate"].

If I don't specify a market, ask before drafting rather than defaulting to one.

variations.label: Internal-only project (not customer-facing)
variations.whenToUse: Use for a project meant for internal documents — memos, reports, Slack updates — where the audience is colleagues, not customers, and the rules differ accordingly.
variations.prompt:
You are the writing assistant for internal communications at [COMPANY NAME]. Audience: [INTERNAL AUDIENCE, e.g. "my direct team of 8, all technical"].

VOICE: [e.g. "terse, bullet-heavy, assume shared context, skip pleasantries"].

HARD RULES:
- Never soften bad news for an internal audience — say what's actually true
- Flag anything that should probably go to legal or HR review instead of being sent as-is
- Default length: [LENGTH RULE]

When I give a task, state the audience and purpose in one line before drafting.

followUps.label: Output still sounds generic? Point at the drift
followUps.prompt: This still doesn't sound like my brand — it reads generic. Compare it directly against the sample documents in the project knowledge and tell me the 3 specific ways it differs (word choice, sentence length, structure), then rewrite it closer to the samples.

followUps.label: Update the instructions, not just this chat
followUps.prompt: That's the right fix. Now write me the exact line I should add to the project's custom instructions so every future chat gets this right automatically, instead of me correcting it each time.

followUps.label: Check it didn't invent anything
followUps.prompt: Go through this draft line by line and flag anything — a feature, a number, a claim — that isn't directly supported by the project knowledge or what I told you in this chat.

followUps.label: Test with a harder, more ambiguous request
followUps.prompt: Now try a harder test: [DELIBERATELY VAGUE OR TRICKY REQUEST]. If the instructions are solid, this should still come out on-brand without me adding more detail.

claude-i1-on-brand-project.walkthrough:
Tomas runs a three-person web design studio and is tired of re-explaining his tone every time he asks Claude for a client email. He decides to build a Project — a workspace inside Claude that holds standing instructions and reference files, loaded automatically into every new chat inside it.

He opens claude.ai, clicks Projects in the sidebar, and creates one named 'Studio — Client Writing.' In the project's custom instructions field, he pastes the template from the lesson, filling in: company name 'Ferro Studio,' business description 'a 3-person web design studio for small local businesses,' audience 'small business owners, usually not technical, often nervous about cost,' tone 'plain and reassuring, never salesy,' preferred term 'project' instead of 'ticket,' required element 'always name the next concrete step.' He then uploads three emails he considers his best work as project knowledge, so Claude has real examples rather than just his adjectives.

He opens a new chat inside the project and types a deliberately vague test: 'Write a short update email about the delayed logo revisions.' The reply comes back sounding calm and specific, opens by naming the delay honestly, and ends with a concrete next step — exactly the pattern from his uploaded samples.

One phrase still feels slightly stiff, so he sends a follow-up: 'The second sentence sounds more formal than my samples — compare it against them and adjust.' The revision matches his voice much better.

Total setup time: about fifteen minutes. Every email he writes in that project from now on starts already sounding like him.

placeholders.name: N
placeholders.what: The number of documents you're uploading, written as a digit. It tells Claude how many files to expect and cross-reference, which matters when file names alone don't make the count obvious.

placeholders.name: FILE 1 NAME
placeholders.what: The exact file name of your first document as it appears after uploading, including the extension. Using the real file name lets Claude refer back to it precisely instead of a vague 'the first document.'
examples: VendorQuote_FastShip.pdf
Lease_Draft_v2.docx
InterviewNotes_CandidateA.txt

placeholders.name: FILE 2 NAME
placeholders.what: The exact file name of your second document, same rule as above — copy it exactly as uploaded.
examples: VendorQuote_RegionalExpress.pdf
Lease_Draft_v3_Landlord_Redline.docx
InterviewNotes_CandidateB.txt

placeholders.name: FILE 3 NAME
placeholders.what: The exact file name of your third document, if you have one. If you're only comparing two files, remove this line from the prompt entirely rather than leaving it blank.
examples: VendorQuote_NorthCargo.pdf
Lease_Final_Landlord_Signed.pdf
InterviewNotes_CandidateC.txt

placeholders.name: TOPIC
placeholders.what: The shared subject all the documents relate to, in a few words. This confirms to Claude — and to you, checking your own setup — that the files genuinely overlap enough to be worth comparing.
examples: national courier contract options
the office lease renewal terms
candidates for the backend developer role

placeholders.name: DECISION
placeholders.what: The actual choice this comparison needs to support — the reason you're doing this analysis at all. A stated decision keeps every section of the output oriented toward what matters, rather than a neutral, unfocused comparison.
examples: which courier to shortlist for a one-year contract
whether to accept the landlord's latest redline or push back on clause 9
which candidate to advance to a final interview

variations.label: Two documents only, quick version
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're comparing exactly two documents and want a lighter version without the full 4-section structure — useful for quick redline checks.
variations.prompt:
I've uploaded 2 documents: [FILE 1 NAME] and [FILE 2 NAME]. Both relate to [TOPIC].

Compare them directly: what changed between them, clause by clause where relevant. For each change, quote both versions and rate its significance for [DECISION] as high/medium/low. Use only what's in the documents — no outside knowledge.

variations.label: Many documents, category-by-category comparison
variations.whenToUse: Use when you have more than 4 files (the tool accepts up to 20) and a flat conflicts table would get unwieldy — group the comparison by theme instead.
variations.prompt:
I've uploaded [N] documents, all relating to [TOPIC]: [LIST ALL FILE NAMES]. I need to decide [DECISION].

Instead of comparing them document by document, organize the analysis by theme: identify the [NUMBER, e.g. "4-6"] recurring topics across all the documents (e.g. pricing, timeline, liability), and for each theme, produce a mini-table showing what each document says, with agreements and conflicts flagged.

End with which document is strongest overall for [DECISION] and why, citing specific themes.

Use only what's in the documents; attribute every claim to its source file.

variations.label: Tracking changes between two versions of the same document
variations.whenToUse: Use specifically for redlines or draft revisions of one document over time, where the goal is tracking what changed, not comparing independent options.
variations.prompt:
I've uploaded two versions of the same document: [FILE 1 NAME — earlier version] and [FILE 2 NAME — newer version]. Topic: [TOPIC].

Produce a change log: every substantive difference between the two versions, organized by section, with the old wording and new wording quoted side by side. Mark each change as favorable to me, unfavorable to me, or neutral, given that I am [YOUR ROLE, e.g. "the tenant"]. Flag anything removed entirely from the newer version — deletions are easy to miss.

End with a recommendation on [DECISION].

followUps.label: Verify a conflict against the actual source
followUps.prompt: For the conflict you listed about [TOPIC OF THE CONFLICT], quote the exact surrounding paragraph from each document so I can check your reading against the original wording myself.

followUps.label: Too many conflicts to act on — rank them
followUps.prompt: There are more conflicts here than I can address at once. Rank all the CONFLICTS rows by how much they actually affect [DECISION], highest impact first, and tell me which 2-3 I should resolve before anything else matters.

followUps.label: Push on a gap that concerns you
followUps.prompt: The GAPS section mentions that [FILE NAME] doesn't address [TOPIC]. Is that actually a meaningful omission for my decision, or just something that document didn't need to cover? Give me your honest read, not just the flag.

followUps.label: Get the synthesis in plainer language
followUps.prompt: Rewrite the SYNTHESIS section in plain, non-technical language, as if you were explaining this to someone with 5 minutes and no background on the documents.

claude-i2-multi-document-analysis.walkthrough:
Elena manages procurement for a mid-size clinic and needs to choose between three competing equipment-maintenance contracts before the end of the month. Each vendor sent their own PDF, worded differently, and she's read them twice without confidently spotting the real differences.

She opens a new Claude chat and uploads all three PDFs using the paperclip icon — MedTech_Contract.pdf, CareServ_Contract.pdf, and Precision_Contract.pdf. She pastes the comparison prompt, filling in 3 documents, the three file names, topic 'equipment maintenance contract terms,' decision 'which vendor to sign a 2-year contract with.'

Claude returns four sections. AGREEMENTS notes all three include quarterly inspections. CONFLICTS is a table showing MedTech offers same-day emergency response but at a higher base fee, while the other two both say '48-hour response' with no same-day option at all. GAPS flags that only Precision's contract mentions what happens if a part needs replacing versus repair — the others are silent, something Elena hadn't noticed on her own reads.

She sends a follow-up: 'Quote the exact same-day response clause from MedTech's contract so I can check it against the original.' Claude quotes the paragraph verbatim; Elena finds it in the PDF and confirms the wording matches.

She then asks for the synthesis, which recommends MedTech given the clinic's history of urgent equipment failures, while flagging the parts-replacement gap as a question to raise with the other two vendors before signing anything. Total time: about twelve minutes, versus the ninety minutes she'd spent re-reading the PDFs the day before.

placeholders.name: TOOL TYPE, e.g. "project quote calculator"
placeholders.what: What kind of interactive tool you want built, described in a few words. Be specific about its purpose rather than generic — 'calculator' alone leaves too much for Claude to guess.
examples: wedding photography package price estimator
employee onboarding checklist with progress tracking
simple event countdown page for a product launch

placeholders.name: WHO WILL USE IT, e.g. "my freelance clients"
placeholders.what: Who will actually interact with the tool — this shapes the language, complexity, and assumptions baked into the design. A tool for your internal team can be denser than one for first-time customers.
examples: prospective clients filling this out before our first call
new hires during their first week
my own team during weekly planning, not customer-facing

placeholders.name: INPUT 1, e.g. "Number of pages (1-50)"
placeholders.what: The first piece of information the tool asks the user for, including its valid range or type. Precise ranges let Claude build sensible validation from the start.
examples: Event date (date picker)
Household size (1-8 people)
Package type: starter / growth / enterprise

placeholders.name: INPUT 2, e.g. "Design complexity: basic / standard / premium"
placeholders.what: The second input field and its allowed values or format. If it's a multiple-choice field, list the exact options — that's what appears in the tool's dropdown or buttons.
examples: Hours of coverage (4, 6, or 8)
Room count (1-10)
Add-ons: none / rush delivery / extra revisions (checkboxes, multiple allowed)

placeholders.name: INPUT 3, e.g. "Rush delivery: yes/no"
placeholders.what: A third input, if needed — often a yes/no toggle, a discount code field, or a smaller detail that modifies the main calculation. Not every tool needs three inputs; add more or fewer as the task requires.
examples: Travel distance in km
Existing client: yes/no (existing clients get a loyalty discount)
Number of participants (1-100)

placeholders.name: RULE 1, e.g. "Base price 120 EUR per page"
placeholders.what: Your actual pricing or logic rule, stated as an exact number or formula — not a description of how pricing generally works. This is the most important line in the whole prompt; a vague rule here produces a tool with invented numbers.
examples: Base rate: 250 EUR per hour of coverage
Starter package: 49 USD/month per 10 users
Base fee: 80 EUR flat, plus 15 EUR per additional guest over 20

placeholders.name: RULE 2, e.g. "Complexity multiplier: basic x1, standard x1.4, premium x1.9"
placeholders.what: A second rule showing exactly how one of your inputs modifies the price — a multiplier, a fixed add-on, or a tiered rate. State the precise numbers for every option, not just the general idea.
examples: Existing client discount: 10% off the base rate
Room count discount: 5% off per room above 5
Add-on pricing: rush delivery +20%, extra revisions +15 EUR each

placeholders.name: RULE 3, e.g. "Rush adds 25% to the total"
placeholders.what: A third rule if your logic needs one — often a surcharge, a minimum charge, or a cap. Leave it out of the prompt entirely if your tool only needs two rules.
examples: Minimum charge: 100 EUR regardless of calculated total
Travel surcharge: free under 30km, then 0.60 EUR/km
Group discount: 10% off if participants exceed 50

placeholders.name: BRAND COLOR
placeholders.what: Your brand's accent color, as a name or hex code, used for buttons, totals, and highlights in the tool. A named color works, but a hex code guarantees an exact match if you know it.
examples: #1B4332 (our forest green)
navy blue, similar to our logo
coral pink, #FF6F61

variations.label: Checklist-style artifact instead of a calculator
variations.whenToUse: Use when the tool you need tracks progress through steps rather than computing a number — onboarding, project kickoffs, event planning.
variations.prompt:
Build an interactive artifact: a checklist for [PROCESS, e.g. "new client onboarding"] used by [WHO WILL USE IT].

Steps to include, in order:
- [STEP 1]
- [STEP 2]
- [STEP 3]
- [STEP 4]

Each step should be checkable, and show a progress indicator (e.g. '2 of 4 complete') that updates as items are checked. Include a short one-line explanation under any step that isn't self-explanatory: [ANY STEPS NEEDING EXPLANATION].

Design: clean, works on mobile, [BRAND COLOR] as the accent color.

variations.label: Read-only interactive explainer, not a calculator
variations.whenToUse: Use when you want an engaging one-page document with interactive elements like tabs or expandable sections, rather than something that computes a result.
variations.prompt:
Build an interactive artifact: a one-page explainer of [TOPIC, e.g. "how our 3-step onboarding process works"] for [WHO WILL SEE THIS].

Structure: [SECTION 1], [SECTION 2], [SECTION 3] — use expandable sections or tabs so it isn't a wall of text.

Include these exact facts, and no others: [FACTS TO INCLUDE].

Design: clean and professional, [BRAND COLOR] as the accent color, readable on mobile. Keep the total text under [WORD LIMIT] words across all sections.

variations.label: Iterating on an existing artifact with a bug
variations.whenToUse: Use this follow-up-style prompt when a previously built artifact has a specific calculation or logic error you've identified through testing.
variations.prompt:
The artifact has a bug: when I set [SPECIFIC INPUT COMBINATION, e.g. "complexity to premium and rush to yes"], the total shows [WRONG BEHAVIOR, e.g. "a negative number"] instead of the correct calculation.

The correct behavior should be: [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN].

Fix only this issue — don't change anything else about the design or other calculations. After fixing it, tell me which other input combinations I should test to make sure the same bug isn't hiding elsewhere.

followUps.label: Total doesn't match a rule? Point at the exact case
followUps.prompt: I tested [SPECIFIC INPUTS] and the total came out to [WRONG NUMBER], but by my own math it should be [CORRECT NUMBER]. Walk through the calculation step by step and find where it diverges from the rules I gave you, then fix it.

followUps.label: Looks good but feels unfinished — polish pass
followUps.prompt: The logic is solid now. Give it a polish pass: add sensible default values so it doesn't start empty, tighten the spacing and alignment, and make the final total visually the most prominent thing on the screen.

followUps.label: Make one small text change without breaking anything
followUps.prompt: Just change the heading text to '[NEW HEADING]' — don't touch any of the calculation logic, inputs, or styling.

followUps.label: Stress-test with an edge case
followUps.prompt: Test it yourself with these edge-case inputs and tell me what happens: all fields left empty, the maximum allowed value in every field at once, and a negative number typed into a numeric field.

claude-i3-build-artifacts.walkthrough:
Nadia runs a small event-catering business and spends too much time on the phone quoting prices for one-off inquiries. She decides to build a quote calculator as a Claude artifact — an artifact being a document or small working tool that Claude can build and show in a live preview panel next to the chat, instead of just describing it in text.

She opens a new chat and writes a brief following the lesson's structure: tool type 'catering quote calculator,' audience 'potential clients filling this in before they call me,' inputs 'guest count (10-300), event type: casual / formal / plated dinner, add-ons: bar service / dessert table / servers (checkboxes).' Her real pricing rules: base rate 28 EUR per guest, formal adds 15%, plated dinner adds 30%, each add-on is a flat 4 EUR per guest. Brand color 'burgundy, #7B2D3E.'

The artifact appears in the side panel — she enters 80 guests, formal, with bar service, and watches the itemized total update live. It looks right, but she notices zero guests shows a total of 'NaN' instead of handling it gracefully.

She sends a follow-up: 'Zero or empty guest count shows NaN — it should show a message asking to enter a number instead.' Claude fixes it immediately in the same artifact.

She tests one more edge case — 300 guests, every add-on checked — confirms the math against her own calculator, then publishes the artifact and sends the link to her business partner to review. Total time: about eighteen minutes for a tool she'll use for months.

placeholders.name: NAME, e.g. "Client status update from raw notes"
placeholders.what: A short, descriptive name for the workflow you're packaging — what you'd call it if you were labeling a folder on your desktop. It should describe the transformation from input to output, not just a vague topic.
examples: Candidate screening summary from interview notes
Weekly ops report from delivery data
Meeting notes to client-ready recap

placeholders.name: PRECISE TRIGGER, e.g. "I ask to turn project notes or a work log into a client-facing status update"
placeholders.what: The exact situation that should make this skill activate, described the way you'd naturally phrase the request on a busy day. This sentence is what Claude matches against, so vague triggers mean the skill fires unreliably.
examples: I paste raw interview notes and ask for a candidate screening summary
I ask to turn a delivery-performance export into a weekly ops report
I paste meeting notes or a transcript and ask for a client recap

placeholders.name: DESCRIBE YOUR STEPS, e.g. "1. Pull out completed items, in-progress items, and blockers. 2. Rewrite in client-friendly language — no internal jargon or team-member blame. 3. Add a 'what we need from you' section if anything is waiting on the client. 4. Keep it under 250 words."
placeholders.what: Your actual current manual process, written as numbered steps, exactly as you do it today — not an idealized version. This is the most important input; a skill is only as good as the real procedure it encodes.
examples: 1. List each candidate's years of experience against the role's must-haves. 2. Note any gap honestly. 3. Score communication only from direct evidence in the notes. 4. End with advance/hold/reject and one sentence why.
1. Pull total deliveries, on-time percentage, and top 3 delay causes. 2. Compare this week to last week. 3. Flag any route with more than 2 late deliveries. 4. Write a 150-word summary for Slack.
1. Separate what was decided from what was discussed. 2. List action items with owner and deadline, or mark unassigned. 3. Rewrite in plain client language. 4. End with a one-paragraph recap.

placeholders.name: RULE 1, e.g. "Never mention internal staffing issues"
placeholders.what: A hard constraint the output must always follow, no matter what — something that would be a real problem if it slipped through even once. State it as an absolute rule, not a preference.
examples: Never infer anything about a candidate's protected characteristics — base every judgment only on stated evidence
Never round percentages in a way that would hide a decline
Never mention which team member caused a delay by name in client-facing output

placeholders.name: RULE 2, e.g. "Every blocker must state what unblocks it"
placeholders.what: A second hard rule your process depends on — often something you've been burned by skipping in the past. If you've corrected an output for this exact reason before, it belongs here.
examples: Every 'hold' or 'reject' recommendation must cite the specific evidence it's based on
Every flagged route must show the actual delay count, not just 'some delays'
Every action item without a stated deadline must say 'NO DEADLINE', never a guessed one

placeholders.name: PASTE EXAMPLE
placeholders.what: A real finished output you consider excellent — the actual text, not a description of what makes it good. This is what Claude derives the output template from, so the more representative it is of your real standard, the better the skill will be.
examples: Candidate: Maria Lund. Experience: 6 years backend, meets all 3 must-haves. Gap: no direct Kubernetes experience, though she has Docker. Communication: clear, structured answers. Recommendation: ADVANCE — strong technical fit, gap is trainable.

Week of Aug 4: 1,204 deliveries, 94% on-time (up from 91%). Top delay cause: warehouse dispatch delays (6 of 9 late orders). Route 12 flagged: 3 late deliveries this week, second week in a row — recommend review.

SUMMARY: Repeated unresolved export bug plus a routine seat question. TEAM: TEAM A. SEVERITY: high. CHURN_RISK: yes — 'we're moving to a competitor'. SUGGESTED_FIRST_REPLY: We're escalating today and will update within 24 hours.

variations.label: Building the skill from scratch with no proven prompt yet
variations.whenToUse: Use when you haven't yet nailed down a working prompt for the task through repeated manual use — this variation has Claude help you develop the process first, before packaging it.
variations.prompt:
I want to build a Claude Skill for [WORKFLOW NAME], but I haven't fully nailed down my process yet — I've only done it manually 1-2 times.

Here's roughly what I do: [ROUGH DESCRIPTION].
Here's one example input and the output I eventually settled on: [INPUT] → [OUTPUT].

First, help me tighten this into a repeatable procedure — ask me questions about any step that seems inconsistent or judgment-based. Only after we've agreed on a stable procedure, draft the SKILL.md.

variations.label: Updating an existing skill after it misfires
variations.whenToUse: Use when a skill you already built is activating incorrectly or producing output that drifted from the template, and needs a targeted fix.
variations.prompt:
My existing skill '[SKILL NAME]' isn't working right. The problem: [PROBLEM, e.g. "it doesn't activate when I phrase the request slightly differently"].

Here's the current SKILL.md: [PASTE CURRENT SKILL.MD]

Here's an example of it misfiring: [WHAT I TYPED] → [WHAT WENT WRONG].

Diagnose whether this is an activation problem (fix the description) or an output problem (fix the procedure or template), then give me the corrected section only — don't rewrite parts that are working.

followUps.label: Skill isn't activating — sharpen the trigger
followUps.prompt: I tried a natural phrasing of this request and the skill didn't activate. Here's exactly what I typed: [WHAT YOU TYPED]. Rewrite the one-line description to more reliably match phrasing like this, without making it so broad it fires on unrelated requests.

followUps.label: Output ignores one of my hard rules
followUps.prompt: The output from testing broke rule [RULE NUMBER] — it did [WHAT WENT WRONG]. Tighten the SKILL.md so this rule is impossible to miss, and explain what in the current wording let it slip through.

followUps.label: Test with a deliberately unrelated request
followUps.prompt: Now show me what would happen if I gave you this unrelated request instead: [UNRELATED REQUEST]. Confirm the skill correctly does NOT activate, and if it would, tell me how to narrow the trigger description.

followUps.label: Simplify an over-engineered first draft
followUps.prompt: This SKILL.md feels longer than it needs to be. Identify anything that's redundant with what a good example already demonstrates, and cut it — the goal is the shortest version that still produces consistent output.

claude-i4-claude-skills.walkthrough:
Simon manages operations for a small courier company and every Monday manually turns the weekend's delivery-exception report into a plain-language summary for his team's stand-up. He's done this the same way for months and decides to turn it into a Claude Skill — a reusable instruction package that Claude automatically loads whenever a matching task comes up, instead of him pasting a long prompt every week.

He checks Settings to confirm Skills are enabled on his plan, then opens a chat and uses the packaging prompt from the lesson. Workflow name: 'Weekend exception report to stand-up summary.' Trigger: 'I paste a delivery-exception CSV or its contents and ask for the Monday summary.' His steps: count total exceptions, group by cause, flag any driver or route appearing more than twice, write under 120 words for a verbal stand-up. Hard rules: never name a driver by name in the summary — group by route only, and always state the total exception count first. He pastes last week's actual summary as the example output.

Claude drafts a SKILL.md with a precise trigger description and warns that a too-similar future trigger, like 'summarize this data,' might also accidentally activate it — suggesting tighter wording, which Simon adopts.

He creates the skill, then tests it the following Monday by pasting the new CSV and simply typing 'stand-up summary please.' It activates immediately and produces a summary matching his format exactly, grouped by route, no names.

Total setup time: about twenty minutes once, replacing roughly fifteen minutes of manual work every week going forward.

placeholders.name: WHO YOU ARE AND THE SITUATION, e.g. "I run a 12-person design agency considering opening a second office"
placeholders.what: Your role and the real-world situation driving this research, in one sentence. This anchors every finding to your actual context instead of a generic overview of the topic.
examples: I'm the ops lead at a 25-person SaaS company evaluating a move to a new payroll provider
I run a solo tax-prep practice deciding whether to specialize in a niche
I'm on the board of a small nonprofit weighing whether to accept cryptocurrency donations

placeholders.name: DECISION, e.g. "choose between Lisbon and Valencia by end of month"
placeholders.what: The specific choice this research needs to resolve, with a timeframe if there is one. Naming the decision, not just the topic, keeps every part of the research oriented toward something actionable.
examples: choose a new payroll provider by the end of the quarter
decide whether tax specialization is worth the retraining cost, within 2 months
vote yes or no on accepting crypto donations at next month's board meeting

placeholders.name: QUESTION 1
placeholders.what: The first specific, answerable sub-question your decision depends on. Break your topic into questions you could imagine getting a real answer to, not just restating the topic.
examples: What do the top 3 payroll providers in our size range actually charge, including hidden fees?
What's the realistic first-year income range for tax specialists in this niche?
What are the tax and reporting obligations for a US nonprofit accepting cryptocurrency?

placeholders.name: QUESTION 2
placeholders.what: A second sub-question, ideally covering a different angle than the first — cost versus risk, near-term versus long-term.
examples: How reliable is each provider's customer support, based on recent user reviews?
What does the retraining or certification path actually require in time and money?
What have similar-sized nonprofits experienced after accepting crypto — any documented problems?

placeholders.name: QUESTION 3
placeholders.what: A third sub-question rounding out the picture. Three is often enough — resist the urge to list ten, which produces a shallow pass over each instead of a real answer to a few.
examples: What are current customers' most common complaints about switching providers mid-year?
Which adjacent skills would make this specialization more defensible against AI-driven commoditization?
What conversion and volatility risk does holding crypto donations even briefly expose us to?

placeholders.name: TIME PERIOD, e.g. "2024 or newer data"
placeholders.what: How recent the information needs to be to count as relevant. This filters out outdated sources that would otherwise get cited with the same confidence as current ones.
examples: 2025 or newer data only
the last 12 months
anything published after the most recent regulation change in March

placeholders.name: GEOGRAPHY/SEGMENT
placeholders.what: The geographic region or market segment your research should focus on, so results aren't diluted with irrelevant regions or company sizes.
examples: US-based providers only, serving companies under 50 employees
Southern Europe, focused on second-tier cities not capitals
small nonprofits under $2M annual budget, US-based

placeholders.name: OUT OF SCOPE, e.g. "remote-only setups"
placeholders.what: What to explicitly exclude — a category that would otherwise sneak into the results and dilute the relevant findings. Naming exclusions is as useful as naming what to include.
examples: enterprise-tier providers meant for 500+ employee companies
international tax specializations outside the US
donation platforms that only support Bitcoin, not other cryptocurrencies

placeholders.name: e.g. "official statistics, government portals, established business press"
placeholders.what: The types of sources you trust most for this research, so Claude weighs them appropriately over marketing content or forum posts. This appears next to the 'SOURCES:' label in the prompt.
examples: official provider documentation, independent review sites like G2 or Capterra, and small-business finance publications
IRS guidance, state CPA board publications, and established tax-industry trade press
IRS/FinCEN guidance, nonprofit sector associations, and major-outlet reporting — not crypto industry blogs

variations.label: Fast version for a lower-stakes decision
variations.whenToUse: Use when the decision matters but doesn't warrant a full multi-question brief — you want current, cited information quickly without the plan-first checkpoint.
variations.prompt:
Quick research brief — use web search and cite sources:

Question: [YOUR QUESTION]
Why it matters: [DECISION IT SUPPORTS]
Time period: [TIME PERIOD]

Give me: a direct answer with citations, one line noting if sources disagreed, and one line on how confident I should be in this answer (well-established / thin evidence).

variations.label: Competitive or comparative research brief
variations.whenToUse: Use when the decision is fundamentally a comparison between named options — competitors, vendors, tools — rather than an open research question.
variations.prompt:
I need to compare specific options for a decision. Use web search and cite sources.

CONTEXT: [SITUATION]. DECISION: [DECISION].
OPTIONS TO COMPARE: [OPTION A], [OPTION B], [OPTION C].

For each option, research: [DIMENSION 1, e.g. "pricing"], [DIMENSION 2, e.g. "customer satisfaction"], [DIMENSION 3, e.g. "reliability track record"].

DELIVERABLE: a comparison table with a source link per cell where possible, followed by a recommendation with reasoning. Label each cell's confidence: WELL-ESTABLISHED, SINGLE-SOURCE, or UNCERTAIN.

Show me your research plan first, in 5 lines or fewer.

followUps.label: Push on the weakest evidence
followUps.prompt: You labeled [SPECIFIC FINDING] as SINGLE-SOURCE or UNCERTAIN. Search specifically for a second independent source that either confirms or contradicts it, and tell me which happened.

followUps.label: Too much reading — give me the bottom line
followUps.prompt: Compress this into exactly 5 bullet points: the finding that most supports my decision, the finding that most argues against it, and the single biggest uncertainty I should know I'm accepting if I decide now.

followUps.label: Check a specific citation
followUps.prompt: Open the source behind [SPECIFIC CLAIM] and confirm: does it actually say what your summary says, and what's the publication date? Quote the exact relevant sentence.

followUps.label: What would change the recommendation?
followUps.prompt: If one of your UNCERTAIN or SINGLE-SOURCE findings turned out to be wrong, which one would most change your recommendation, and what evidence would I need to see to know that?

claude-i5-deep-research-briefs.walkthrough:
Karolina co-owns a 12-person design agency and is deciding whether to open a second office in Lisbon or Valencia by the end of the month. She's read a few blog posts but doesn't trust the picture they give her.

She opens Claude and writes the full brief: context 'I run a 12-person design agency considering a second office,' decision 'choose between Lisbon and Valencia by end of month,' three key questions covering commercial rent for a small studio space, the local pool of mid-level designers, and the tax treatment of a foreign branch office. Scope: 2025 or newer data, focused on those two cities specifically, explicitly ignoring co-working memberships since she wants a real lease. Sources: official statistics and established business press, treating relocation-consultancy marketing pages as weak evidence.

Claude first shows a five-line research plan — it proposes tackling the tax question first since an unfavorable answer could end the comparison outright. Karolina approves.

The finished report labels average studio rent in both cities as WELL-ESTABLISHED, since multiple listings sites agree, flags one designer-salary figure from a single recruiter's blog as SINGLE-SOURCE, and notes in 'could not verify' that branch-office tax treatment depends on a ruling that varies case by case — recommending she confirm with a local accountant before committing.

She sends one follow-up asking Claude to open the salary source directly; it turns out to be two years old, which she flags as unreliable. She forwards the report to her co-founder along with her own note about the outdated salary figure. Total time: about twenty-five minutes, for a comparison sharper than the blog posts gave her.

placeholders.name: ITEM TYPE, e.g. "customer support requests"
placeholders.what: The category of thing you're triaging or classifying, in a few words. This sets the domain vocabulary the whole prompt operates in.
examples: customer support requests
inbound sales leads
product feedback submissions

placeholders.name: CONTEXT, e.g. "a B2B software company"
placeholders.what: A short description of the business or situation this classification happens within. It calibrates what counts as normal versus a red flag for your specific context.
examples: a B2B software company selling to mid-market retailers
a residential plumbing and HVAC service business
a subscription meal-kit company

placeholders.name: KEY RISK, e.g. "churn risk: mentions of cancelling, competitors, or repeated unresolved issues"
placeholders.what: The specific risk or signal you most need the reasoning to check for before concluding, described precisely enough that Claude knows exactly what language counts as a signal.
examples: safety risk: any mention of injury, gas smell, or electrical sparking
budget risk: mentions of a competitor's price or 'need to check with finance'
urgency risk: mentions of an event date, a broken appliance with no backup, or 'ASAP'

placeholders.name: TEAM A / TEAM B / TEAM C
placeholders.what: The actual names of the teams or categories this item could be routed to, exactly as your organization uses them. List every valid option — Claude should never invent a team name that isn't one of these.
examples: Technical Support / Billing / Sales
Plumbing / HVAC / Electrical
Kitchen Team / Delivery Team / Customer Care

placeholders.name: PASTE INPUT
placeholders.what: The actual raw text — the message, request, or feedback item — you want triaged, pasted in full. Paste one item at a time when testing, so you can verify each output individually before running a batch.
examples: Hi, I've called twice about the AC not cooling below 78 even on full blast, and no one's called me back. My elderly mother lives here and it's 95 out. Can someone come today?
This is the second time your competitor's rep mentioned they'd match your price. We like your product but need to see a discount conversation before renewal, or we'll consider switching.
Loved the beef stir-fry kit! Only issue: the sauce packet was torn open and leaked in the box. Everything else was fine, wasn't a big deal, just wanted to flag it.

variations.label: Scoring instead of routing
variations.whenToUse: Use this version when the task is ranking or scoring items on a scale, like leads or applications, rather than routing them to a team.
variations.prompt:
You score incoming [ITEM TYPE] for [CONTEXT].

REASONING ORDER:
1. Identify the core need or intent behind the item.
2. Check it against these fit criteria: [FIT CRITERIA, e.g. "company size 50-500, stated budget, decision-maker involved"].
3. Only then assign a score.

OUTPUT CONTRACT — exactly these fields:
SCORE: 1-5 (5 = strongest fit)
FIT_REASON: one sentence, tied to the fit criteria
NEXT_ACTION: exactly one of [ACTION A, ACTION B, ACTION C]

If a fit criterion can't be assessed from the input, note it in FIT_REASON as 'insufficient info on X' rather than guessing a score.

EXAMPLE
Input: [WORKED EXAMPLE INPUT]
Output:
SCORE: [EXAMPLE SCORE]
FIT_REASON: [EXAMPLE REASON]
NEXT_ACTION: [EXAMPLE ACTION]

Now process:
[PASTE INPUT]

variations.label: Two-example version for edge-case-heavy tasks
variations.whenToUse: Use when a single example doesn't disambiguate the tricky boundary cases — pairing a typical example with a tricky one teaches the distinction better than either alone.
variations.prompt:
[SAME SETUP AS MAIN PROMPT: ITEM TYPE, CONTEXT, REASONING ORDER, OUTPUT CONTRACT]

EXAMPLE 1 — typical case:
Input: [TYPICAL INPUT]
Output: [TYPICAL OUTPUT]

EXAMPLE 2 — tricky case handled correctly:
Input: [TRICKY INPUT THAT COULD BE MISCLASSIFIED]
Output: [CORRECT OUTPUT, WITH THE RIGHT CALL EXPLAINED]

Now process:
[PASTE INPUT]

followUps.label: Fields came back inconsistent — enforce the contract
followUps.prompt: The TEAM field in that output wasn't one of my three allowed values. Reprocess the same input, and this time if none of the three teams clearly fit, use TEAM_UNCLEAR rather than inventing a new category.

followUps.label: Reasoning skipped a step — show your work
followUps.prompt: Show me which of the 4 reasoning-order steps led to this SEVERITY rating, quoting the specific phrase in my input that triggered it. If no phrase triggered it, tell me honestly that the rating was closer to a guess.

followUps.label: Test it against a tricky edge case
followUps.prompt: Now process this deliberately ambiguous input using the exact same contract, and tell me honestly if any field required a judgment call rather than being clear-cut: [PASTE TRICKY INPUT]

followUps.label: Tighten the example to fix a recurring mistake
followUps.prompt: Across the last few outputs, [SPECIFIC FIELD] keeps coming out wrong in the same way: [DESCRIBE THE PATTERN]. Suggest a change to the worked example that would correct this pattern, then show me the corrected example.

claude-i6-advanced-prompting-contracts.walkthrough:
Ben runs support operations for a small software company and wants inbound tickets triaged consistently before they hit his team's queue — right now, three different people write summaries in three different formats, making it hard to spot patterns.

He builds the prompt using the lesson's template: item type 'customer support tickets,' context 'a B2B project-management software company,' key risk 'churn risk: mentions of cancelling, competitors, or repeated unresolved issues,' teams 'Technical / Billing / Onboarding.' He writes the output contract with SUMMARY, TEAM, SEVERITY, CHURN_RISK, and SUGGESTED_FIRST_REPLY fields, each with exact allowed values, plus the missing-data rule. He includes one worked example showing a ticket that mentions both a bug and a billing question, correctly routed to Technical since that's the more severe issue.

He tests it on a real backlog of five tickets. Four come back in the identical format, easy to scan. The fifth, a ticket mentioning a competitor's name in passing and unrelated to any complaint, gets marked CHURN_RISK: yes incorrectly.

He sends a follow-up: 'That churn risk flag is wrong — the competitor mention was casual, not a threat to leave. Tighten the example so a bare competitor mention isn't automatically a churn signal.' Claude revises the example to include a case exactly like this, correctly marked CHURN_RISK: no.

He reruns the same five tickets; all five now come back correctly and consistently formatted. Total setup time: about twenty-five minutes, and every ticket from then on arrives in his queue pre-sorted the same way, whoever wrote it.

placeholders.name: "a verbatim transcript with speaker labels" / "my own rough notes"
placeholders.what: Tell Claude which kind of raw material you're providing, since the two require different handling — a verbatim transcript can be quoted directly, while rough notes need more cautious inference. Pick whichever phrase actually describes what you're pasting.
examples: a verbatim transcript with speaker labels
my own rough notes, not a full transcript
a mix — an auto-generated transcript with a few of my own annotations added

placeholders.name: PURPOSE, e.g. "weekly project sync for the website relaunch"
placeholders.what: What kind of meeting this was and its recurring purpose, in a short phrase. This tells Claude what counts as a normal agenda item versus something noteworthy.
examples: weekly project sync for the website relaunch
quarterly budget review with department heads
first client kickoff call for a new engagement

placeholders.name: NAMES AND ROLES
placeholders.what: Who attended and what each person's role or authority is, especially anyone who can actually confirm a decision. This is essential for the DECISIONS section — Claude needs to know who has the standing to make something official.
examples: Elena (design lead, can approve visual direction), Marcus (client-side project owner), Tom (developer, no decision authority)
Sofia (me, project manager), David (finance director, budget sign-off), two department heads observing only
Client: Raj (owner, final decision-maker). Us: me and one designer, presenting only

placeholders.name: PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR NOTES
placeholders.what: The actual raw text of the meeting — paste the whole thing, even messy or informal parts. Trimming it down yourself risks cutting the exact phrase that would have revealed a decision or a missed commitment.
examples: Elena: I think we should go with option B for the homepage. Marcus: agreed, let's lock that in. Tom: I can start Monday but need the final copy first — who's writing that? Elena: I'll get you a draft by Wednesday.

- discussed Q3 budget overrun in marketing, mostly ad spend
- David said he'd look into reallocating from the events line but didn't commit to a number
- someone (Priya?) needs to send updated headcount numbers by Friday
Raj: we want the new site live before our trade show, that's the 14th. Me: that's tight but doable if we get content by the 1st. Raj: I'll have my team send it over this week.

variations.label: Rough personal notes instead of a transcript
variations.whenToUse: Use when you only have your own quick, informal notes rather than a full transcript — this version is more cautious about treating anything as confirmed.
variations.prompt:
Below are my own rough notes from a meeting — not a transcript, so treat anything I've paraphrased as less certain than a direct quote.

Context: [PURPOSE]. Attendees: [NAMES AND ROLES].

Extract DECISIONS, ACTION ITEMS (table: Action | Owner | Deadline), OPEN QUESTIONS, and NOTABLE CONTEXT, keeping categories separate. Since these are my notes, not a transcript, be extra cautious: if something might be my summary of a decision rather than an actual confirmed decision, put it under NEEDS CLARIFICATION instead of DECISIONS.

My notes:
[PASTE YOUR NOTES]

variations.label: Recurring meeting — compare against last time's action items
variations.whenToUse: Use for a recurring meeting series where you want to track whether previous commitments were actually completed, not just extract new ones.
variations.prompt:
Below is [a transcript / my notes] from a recurring meeting: [PURPOSE]. Attendees: [NAMES AND ROLES].

Last meeting's open action items were:
[PASTE PREVIOUS ACTION ITEMS]

First, check the text below for any mention of these previous items — mark each as DONE (with evidence), STILL OPEN, or NOT MENTIONED. Then extract this meeting's new DECISIONS, ACTION ITEMS, OPEN QUESTIONS, and NOTABLE CONTEXT using the same strict rules as before.

Text:
[PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR NOTES]

variations.label: Extracting only action items, fast
variations.whenToUse: Use this stripped-down version when you just need the task list quickly and don't need the full decisions/questions/context breakdown.
variations.prompt:
From the meeting text below, extract ONLY action items as a table: Action | Owner | Deadline | Source quote. Use only owners and deadlines actually stated — mark UNASSIGNED or NO DEADLINE otherwise, never inferred. Nothing else, no summary, no decisions section.

[PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR NOTES]

followUps.label: Double-check an UNASSIGNED item wasn't actually assigned
followUps.prompt: Re-read the section around [ACTION ITEM] one more time — are you sure no owner was stated, even indirectly? Quote the surrounding exchange so I can judge for myself.

followUps.label: Resolve a NEEDS CLARIFICATION item
followUps.prompt: For the item you flagged under NEEDS CLARIFICATION about [TOPIC], give me the full surrounding exchange verbatim, plus your best guess at what was meant — labeled clearly as a guess, not a finding.

followUps.label: Make the follow-up message warmer
followUps.prompt: The follow-up draft is accurate but sounds a bit clinical. Rewrite it slightly warmer, as if from someone who was actually in the room and cares about the project, without losing any of the specifics.

followUps.label: Cross-check total action item count
followUps.prompt: Count how many distinct commitments or 'I'll do X' statements appear in the raw text versus how many made it into your ACTION ITEMS table. If the numbers don't match, tell me what you left out and why.

claude-i7-meetings-to-decisions.walkthrough:
Aisha manages a 6-person product team and just finished a 35-minute planning call, recorded and auto-transcribed with speaker labels by her video tool. Normally she'd spend fifteen minutes after the call writing up notes from memory, and she knows from experience she forgets at least one commitment every time.

She copies the full transcript, opens Claude, and pastes the extraction prompt. She specifies 'a verbatim transcript with speaker labels,' purpose 'biweekly product planning sync,' attendees 'me (Aisha, PM), Raj (lead engineer, can commit engineering time), Priya (designer, no scheduling authority), two engineers observing.'

Claude returns four sections. DECISIONS lists one: feature X ships in the next sprint, confirmed by Raj, quoted directly from the transcript. ACTION ITEMS has five rows, one marked UNASSIGNED — updating the onboarding docs, which two people discussed but neither actually agreed to own. NEEDS CLARIFICATION flags a moment where Priya said 'maybe we push the redesign' and got a vague 'sure, maybe' back — genuinely unclear if that was a decision.

Aisha sends one follow-up: 'Re-read the redesign exchange one more time — quote it fully so I can judge myself.' The quote confirms it really was inconclusive, so she leaves it as an open question rather than assuming either direction.

She assigns the onboarding docs task to herself in the follow-up message Claude drafted, then sends it to the team. Total time: four minutes, versus her usual fifteen, and the UNASSIGNED flag caught exactly the kind of task that used to fall through.

placeholders.name: CONTENT TYPE, e.g. "a practical guide"
placeholders.what: What kind of piece you're writing — its format and general purpose. This sets reader expectations that shape structure; a guide needs steps, an opinion piece needs an argument.
examples: a practical how-to guide
a persuasive opinion piece for our company blog
an internal policy document

placeholders.name: WORKING TITLE
placeholders.what: A draft title, even if it changes later. A working title forces you to state the piece's angle before writing, which sharpens the outline that follows.
examples: Technical SEO for E-commerce Migrations: A Practical Checklist
Why We're Moving to a 4-Day Week (And What Changes)
New Manager's Guide to Running Your First Performance Review

placeholders.name: AUDIENCE
placeholders.what: Who this piece is written for — their existing knowledge level and what they came looking for. This determines what needs explaining versus what can be assumed.
examples: e-commerce marketing managers with some technical familiarity but not developers
our whole company, mixed technical background, some skeptical of the change
first-time managers, no HR training, nervous about the conversation

placeholders.name: WHAT IT MUST ACHIEVE
placeholders.what: The concrete outcome you want a reader to walk away with. Vague purposes like 'raise awareness' produce vague pieces; specific purposes produce focused ones.
examples: give the reader a concrete checklist they can literally follow during their own migration
convince skeptical employees the change is being made thoughtfully, not as a cost-cutting move
leave a new manager confident enough to actually schedule the conversation this week

placeholders.name: N
placeholders.what: Your target word count, as a number. This shapes how much depth each section can have — the outline's per-section word counts should roughly add up to this total.

placeholders.name: KEY POINT 1
placeholders.what: The first idea the piece absolutely must land, stated as a real claim, not just a topic.
examples: Most e-commerce migrations fail from redirect mapping, not from platform choice itself
A 4-day week only works if meeting culture changes first
The opening two minutes of a performance review set the entire tone

placeholders.name: KEY POINT 2
placeholders.what: A second must-land idea, ideally complementary to or building on the first rather than repeating it.
examples: Redirect mapping is solvable with a specific 3-step process most teams skip
Client-facing hours need explicit coverage rules or the change quietly fails
Concrete examples beat general feedback every time

placeholders.name: KEY POINT 3
placeholders.what: A third must-land idea rounding out the argument.
examples: Post-migration monitoring in the first 30 days catches most remaining issues cheaply
This isn't a trial — we're committing, and here's why that matters for planning
Every review should end with one agreed next step, not just impressions

placeholders.name: TONE, e.g. "plain, direct, first person plural"
placeholders.what: The voice the piece should be written in, described concretely enough to apply consistently across every section.
examples: plain, direct, first person plural — 'we' not 'the company'
warm but authoritative, second person, occasional light humor
formal and precise, third person, no contractions

variations.label: Shorter piece, single-pass draft after outline
variations.whenToUse: Use for shorter pieces under 800 words where full section-by-section drafting is overkill — you still want the outline checkpoint, but can draft the whole thing in one pass after approving it.
variations.prompt:
I'm writing [CONTENT TYPE] titled "[WORKING TITLE]" for [AUDIENCE]. Purpose: [WHAT IT MUST ACHIEVE]. Target length: about [N] words (short piece).

It must land: [KEY POINT 1], [KEY POINT 2].

First give me an outline only — section headings with a one-line job for each — and flag any weak point before I approve it. After I approve, write the full piece in one pass, staying within the approved structure, tone [TONE], and marking any fact I haven't given you as [VERIFY].

variations.label: Collaborative piece with a co-author's material to incorporate
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're combining your own material with content from a colleague or subject-matter expert, and need the outline to show where each source's material goes.
variations.prompt:
I'm writing [CONTENT TYPE] titled "[WORKING TITLE]" for [AUDIENCE], combining my own notes with material from a colleague.

My notes: [YOUR NOTES/POINTS]
Colleague's material: [PASTE COLLEAGUE'S NOTES OR DRAFT]

STEP 1 — OUTLINE ONLY. Show me a section-by-section outline, and for each section note whether it draws mainly on my notes, my colleague's material, or needs new synthesis. Flag any place where our material conflicts or overlaps.

After I approve, draft one section at a time, marking clearly with [MY VOICE] or [COLLEAGUE'S VOICE] if the tone needs to differ.

followUps.label: Outline felt thin — push for a sharper through-line
followUps.prompt: The through-line you described feels weak — I'm not sure a reader would feel pulled from section 1 to the conclusion. Propose a sharper through-line, even if it means reordering or merging sections.

followUps.label: Section drifted from its stated job
followUps.prompt: Section [NUMBER] wandered into territory that belongs in section [OTHER NUMBER] — it's supposed to be about [THAT SECTION'S JOB]. Rewrite it to stay within its original scope, and don't preview content from later sections.

followUps.label: Resolve the [VERIFY] flags
followUps.prompt: List every [VERIFY] flag across the piece so far in one place, with the sentence it's attached to. I'll tell you which are true, which are false, and which to cut.

followUps.label: Run the consistency pass now
followUps.prompt: All sections are drafted. Now do the full consistency pass: check for tone drift between sections, any point made twice, any contradiction, and whether the conclusion actually delivers on what the introduction promised.

claude-i8-outline-first-longform.walkthrough:
Daniel writes content for a mid-size accounting software company and has been asked for a 2,000-word guide on year-end closing for small business owners. His past attempts at long pieces have tended to start strong and trail off by the middle.

He opens Claude and writes the brief: content type 'a practical guide,' working title 'Year-End Close Without the Panic: A Small Business Guide,' audience 'small business owners doing their own books, not accountants,' purpose 'give them a checklist they'll actually follow in December, not just background reading,' target length 2000 words. Key points: reconciliation should happen monthly, not just in December; the three most-missed deductions cost real money; a simple pre-close checklist prevents the January scramble. Tone: plain, direct, second person, no jargon without explaining it.

Claude returns an outline-only response — six sections with one-line jobs and word targets — plus a pushback: it notes that the deductions section and the checklist section would overlap heavily and suggests merging the deduction tips directly into the checklist instead. Daniel agrees; it's a smarter structure than his own draft plan.

He approves the outline, then requests sections one at a time, correcting tone in section one immediately when it reads slightly too formal, which keeps every later section consistent with the fix.

After the last section, he asks for the consistency pass, which catches that sections two and five both explain what reconciliation means — he trims the repeat. Total time: just under an hour, for a piece that reads as one continuous argument rather than six stitched-together paragraphs.

placeholders.name: FILENAME
placeholders.what: The exact name of the CSV file you uploaded, so Claude and you are both referring to the same file precisely, especially useful if you upload more than one file across a session.
examples: orders_2025.csv
delivery_performance_q3.csv
survey_results_august.csv

placeholders.name: WHAT THE DATA IS, e.g. "12 months of order data from our online store"
placeholders.what: A one-sentence description of what the dataset actually is and what a single row represents. Column names alone are often ambiguous, so stating this upfront prevents early misreadings.
examples: 12 months of order data from our online store, one row per order
a survey of 340 customers about a new product feature, one row per respondent
delivery logs for Q3, one row per individual delivery attempt

placeholders.name: CLARIFY AMBIGUOUS COLUMNS, e.g. "'revenue' is net of refunds; 'region' is shipping region"
placeholders.what: Any column whose meaning isn't obvious from its name, clarified in plain language. This is the single highest-leverage sentence in the whole prompt — a misread column corrupts every calculation built on it.
examples: 'total' includes tax; 'discount_pct' is stored as a decimal like 0.15, not 15
'response_score' is on a 1-7 scale, not the usual 1-5
'delivered_on_time' is TRUE/FALSE based on the promised window, not the requested date

placeholders.name: DECISION, e.g. "where to focus Q4 marketing spend"
placeholders.what: The actual business decision this analysis needs to inform. Stating it keeps the whole three-phase process oriented toward something actionable rather than a neutral data tour.
examples: where to focus Q4 marketing spend
whether to add more drivers to the two slowest routes
which product feature to prioritize for the next release

placeholders.name: QUESTION 1, e.g. "Which product categories drive the most revenue and how has that mix shifted by quarter?"
placeholders.what: Your first specific analysis question, phrased so it has a computable answer. Vague questions like 'what's interesting here' produce vague, unfocused analysis.
examples: Which product categories drive the most revenue, and how has that mix shifted by quarter?
Which two routes have the most late deliveries, and is the cause dispatch delay or traffic?
Which customer segment gave the lowest satisfaction scores, and what specific complaint comes up most in their comments?

placeholders.name: QUESTION 2
placeholders.what: A second specific analysis question, ideally covering a different angle of the same decision.
examples: Do repeat customers spend more per order than first-time customers, and by how much?
Has on-time delivery improved or worsened month over month?
Is there a relationship between delivery speed and satisfaction score?

placeholders.name: QUESTION 3
placeholders.what: A third specific analysis question rounding out what you need to know before deciding.
examples: Which region shows the strongest growth trend over the past 6 months?
Which driver or route accounts for a disproportionate share of exceptions?
Do respondents who used the feature daily rate it differently than occasional users?

placeholders.name: AUDIENCE, e.g. "our leadership team, non-technical"
placeholders.what: Who the final executive summary is written for, which determines how much statistical detail versus plain-language interpretation belongs in it.
examples: our leadership team, non-technical, cares about the bottom line
the whole ops team, some technical, presented in a Monday meeting
myself and my co-founder, we can handle some detail but want the headline first

variations.label: Quick single-question version
variations.whenToUse: Use when you have one specific question and don't need the full profile-then-analyze-then-summarize pipeline — still keeps the discipline of computing rather than guessing.
variations.prompt:
I've uploaded [FILENAME], which contains [WHAT THE DATA IS]. Column notes: [CLARIFY AMBIGUOUS COLUMNS].

claude-i9-csv-to-executive-summary.walkthrough:
Fatima co-owns a small online homeware shop and needs to decide where to focus Q4 marketing spend. She has a year of order data sitting in a CSV export from her store platform that she's never properly analyzed.

She uploads orders_2025.csv and pastes the three-phase prompt. Filename noted, data description 'a year of order data from our online shop, one row per order,' column notes clarifying that 'total' includes tax and that 'category' sometimes has trailing spaces she's noticed before, decision 'where to focus Q4 marketing spend.'

Phase 1 comes back first: 2,140 rows, a data-quality flag about 31 duplicate order IDs from a known double-export issue, and confirmation of the trailing-space problem in 'category,' with two entries for 'Kitchen' and 'Kitchen '. Fatima replies with her handling choice: drop the exact duplicates, merge the two Kitchen variants.

For phase 2, her three questions ask which category drives the most revenue, whether repeat customers spend more per order, and which region is growing fastest. Claude computes each using code — the analysis tool, meaning it actually runs calculations on her file rather than estimating from a glance — and shows the formula behind each number. Kitchen products turn out to drive 38% of revenue, and repeat customers spend 1.8x more per order on average.

She asks a follow-up to double check the 38% figure's underlying rows, confirms it against her own quick spreadsheet total, and requests the executive summary for her non-technical co-founder. The one-pager recommends concentrating Q4 spend on Kitchen and a retention push for repeat buyers, with a caveats section noting the dropped duplicates. Total time: about twenty minutes.

claude-i10-memory-conversation-strategy.walkthrough:
Owen is a freelance consultant running a six-week operations audit for a client, and previous projects have taught him that a single sprawling chat becomes unusable by week three — he can never find the reasoning behind a decision once it's twenty messages back.

At the start, he opens Settings and reads Claude's memory summary, a short standing note Claude keeps about him across chats, and deletes an outdated line about a past client's industry that no longer applies. He creates a Project called 'Meridian Ops Audit,' and puts the durable facts into its custom instructions: client name, the three departments in scope, the deadline, and the stakeholder list. He uploads the signed engagement letter as project knowledge.

Each work item becomes its own chat, opened with the two-line pointer from the lesson. For the interview-notes-to-findings chat, he writes: task 'drafting initial findings from the warehouse team interviews'; pointers 'scope is warehouse and shipping only per the engagement letter; client wants findings framed as opportunities, not criticisms, per our March 3 kickoff call.'

Claude drafts the findings staying strictly within that scope, and at the end Owen types 'wrap up' — Claude gives him a three-line summary he pastes straight into the project's knowledge as a dated entry.

Three weeks later, the client asks why a particular recommendation was dropped. Owen searches his chat titles, finds 'warehouse interview findings' immediately, and has the reasoning in under a minute, instead of scrolling a single endless thread. Total setup overhead: about ten minutes at the start, saving him real time every week since.

placeholders.name: REVIEWER ROLE, e.g. "client CFO who will challenge anything imprecise"
placeholders.what: The adversarial persona you want Claude to review as — someone with a real reason to poke holes in this specific document. A well-chosen role finds different problems than a generic 'please check this.'
examples: client CFO who will challenge anything imprecise or unsupported
opposing counsel looking for any opening to dispute
an angry customer looking for a reason to escalate this complaint further

placeholders.name: LIST, e.g. "under 400 words, no pricing commitments, formal tone"
placeholders.what: The original requirements you gave when drafting this piece, restated here so the review can check compliance against them specifically, not just general quality.
examples: under 400 words, no pricing commitments, formal tone
must mention the refund policy, friendly but firm tone, no more than 3 short paragraphs
must include the safety disclaimer verbatim, plain language, under 250 words

placeholders.name: PASTE DRAFT
placeholders.what: The actual draft you're about to send, pasted in full. Paste the finished version you intend to use, not an earlier rough version — the review is only as useful as what it's actually checking.
examples: Hi Marcus, following up on our call — I've attached the revised proposal at 45,000 EUR for the full engagement, running March through June. Let me know if the timeline works.

placeholders.name: PASTE SOURCES
placeholders.what: The source material the draft is supposed to be grounded in — the contract, the data, the notes it was based on. This is what the GROUNDING check compares every factual claim against, so include the actual source text, not a summary of it.
examples: Section 4.2: Payment due within 30 days of the effective date, defined in Section 1 as the date both parties countersign. Section 9.1: Client responsible for structural maintenance only.
Settlement Agreement, Clause 3: Payment of $12,000 due within 30 days of the effective date. Clause 7: Release covers claims related to Invoice #2241 only.
Order #8834, refund policy applies: items returned within 30 days, opened or unopened, full refund to original payment method, processed within 5-7 business days per policy page.

claude-i11-quality-control-verification.walkthrough:
Henrik runs a small accounting firm and has drafted a client email confirming the outcome of a tax filing dispute, based on the actual correspondence with the tax authority. Getting a number or date wrong here isn't just embarrassing — it could be a real professional liability.

He pastes the review prompt into Claude, setting reviewer role to 'a skeptical client who will scrutinize every number since money is involved,' his original requirements 'under 200 words, must state the exact amount owed and the payment deadline, calm and reassuring tone.' Below that he pastes his draft email and, as source material, the actual text of the tax authority's decision letter.

The GROUNDING section flags one CONTRADICTED item: his draft says the amount due is '2,340 EUR,' but the source letter states '2,430 EUR', a transposition, quoted side by side. This is exactly the kind of error that reads as completely confident and would have gone out unnoticed. RISKY AMBIGUITY flags his phrase 'this should resolve the matter' as overstating certainty the source doesn't actually support.

Henrik sends a follow-up asking Claude to fix just the amount sentence to match the source exactly. He also manually tightens the 'should resolve' phrase himself, then does one more read of the original decision letter's key paragraph himself, the human check that catches anything a review might still miss on the number that matters most.

He sends the corrected email with real confidence instead of hoping it was right. Total time: about six minutes, for a check that likely saved a serious correction later.

claude-i12-cross-platform-workflow.walkthrough:
Yusuf runs a small property-management business and splits his time between an office, tenant site visits, and driving between properties, so his laptop is often not with him when a task-worthy thought occurs.

He opens Claude on desktop and runs the routing prompt, describing his week honestly: mornings at his desk on lease paperwork and owner reports, afternoons doing site visits and tenant calls, evenings comparing maintenance-contractor quotes across several websites, and ideas about problem properties tend to hit him mid-drive between visits.

The routing plan comes back concrete: capture property issues by voice on mobile immediately after each visit, into the relevant property's Project, rather than trying to remember them until evening; draft owner reports at his desk where he can pull up the captured notes already organized by property; use Claude in Chrome specifically for the contractor-quote comparison, since it involves several open tabs he currently juggles manually. For safety, it recommends keeping his banking and tenant-payment portal tabs closed during any Chrome session where Claude is active, since sites can carry hidden instructions, called prompt injection, that a browsing assistant could be tricked into following.

His two trial habits for the first week: voice-capture after every site visit, and Thursday evening's contractor comparison in Chrome. By the following Thursday, the comparison, normally forty minutes of tab-switching, takes fifteen, and his owner report references specific details from visits he'd previously have half-forgotten by Friday. Total setup time: about twenty minutes for a routing plan he actually keeps using.
